conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team. You’re here because of right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and a low fever. Is that correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. The pain started two days ago. It feels like my past cholangitis episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of primary sclerosing cholangitis, that’s definitely a concern. We’ll start with blood tests to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had this before—should we be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re being cautious. Your symptoms are similar to past infections, so we’ll treat it seriously but step by step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show a low white blood cell count, which can happen with liver disease. Liver enzymes are elevated, especially alkaline phosphatase—consistent with bile duct issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So, is it cholangitis again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely. We’re starting IV antibiotics—meropenem—to cover possible infection, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that one. It’s strong, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s broad-spectrum. We’ll use it until we know more. We also need to check your bile ducts with an ERCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: ERCP? That’s the scope procedure, right? I’ve had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It lets us look inside your ducts and make sure there’s no blockage or stone causing the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. When will it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. We’ll also place a PICC line so you can finish antibiotics at home if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a PICC last time. Is that because the antibiotics take a while?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, usually two weeks. It’s safer and more effective through a vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Your blood cultures came back—no growth so far. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I don’t have an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Sometimes cultures are negative even if there’s infection, especially if it’s low-grade. We’ll keep treating based on your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I still feel achy, so I guess it’s better to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Another blood culture was drawn—still no growth. Your liver numbers are a bit better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a little less nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a positive sign. Your ERCP is scheduled for 10 a.m. Any questions before then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they take pictures? Can they remove anything if there’s a stone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll inject dye to see the ducts clearly. If there’s a blockage, they can often clear it during the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back. The ERCP went well. Good news—your bile duct is open, no stones or blockages seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! So why am I still sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Even without a blockage, you can have inflammation or low-grade infection due to your PSC. We’ll continue antibiotics to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll keep taking them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re placing the PICC line. It’ll go into your arm and reach a large vein near your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get numbing medicine. You might feel pressure, but not sharp pain. An ultrasound guides it, so it’s very precise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC was placed successfully. A chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right spot—mid superior vena cava.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. We’ll switch you from meropenem to ertapenem, which you’ll take once daily through the PICC at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as last time. I remember how to do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll arrange nursing support to help with the first few doses and teach you the flush routine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to mess it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show improvement. White count is still low but stable. Liver enzymes are trending down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your pain is milder, and you’re tolerating food. We’re planning to discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ll be discharged today. We gave one dose of ertapenem this morning, and you’ll continue for 14 days at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll restart rifaximin after finishing ertapenem. Continue your usual meds: ursodiol, omeprazole, furosemide, levothyroxine, and escitalopram.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped rifaximin when I started the IV antibiotics, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. We paused it to avoid overlap. Resume it after the ertapenem course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Call if you develop fever, worsening pain, redness at the PICC site, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Your care team will follow up, and please keep your primary care appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also monitor your blood counts and liver function in follow-up. Anemia is stable, so no changes needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My energy is still low, but I guess that’s from the anemia and everything else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s common. It should improve as you recover. Keep eating well and resting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re discharging you with home health support for the PICC. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I avoid gluten?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. You have celiac disease, so staying gluten-free is important for your gut and liver health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I try to, but sometimes it’s hard when eating out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Just do your best. Even small exposures can cause issues over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be more careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. You’re on the right track.
